**🥉 Basecamp** – Best for simplicity
   To-dos, message boards, docs, schedules, and group chat in a clean interface. Flat pricing ($99/month unlimited users) makes it predictable for small teams.

**🏅 Coda** – Best for "doc-as-app" builders
   Like Notion but with stronger formulas, automations, and pack integrations — great if your team likes building custom lightweight tools.

descriptions.description:
Notion is a productivity software company best known for its flagship app, often just called "Notion." Here's an overview:

**What they do**
Notion offers an all-in-one workspace application that combines several functions into a single tool:
- Notes and document writing
- Databases and tables
- Wikis and knowledge bases
- Task and project management
- Calendars and to-do lists
- Collaborative documents

Its signature feature is a "block-based" editor, where every piece of content (text, images, tables, embeds, etc.) is treated as a movable block. This makes the interface highly flexible and customizable.

**Who they are for**
Notion's audience is broad, spanning:
- Individuals for personal note-taking, journaling, and life organization
- Students for study notes and assignments
- Small teams and startups for project tracking and internal documentation
- Larger enterprises as an internal wiki or company-wide knowledge base
- Writers, researchers, and creators for organizing ideas and references

**Notable points**
- Founded in 2013 by Ivan Zhao, who remains CEO; headquartered in San Francisco.
- Grew rapidly in popularity during the COVID-19 pandemic as remote work expanded.
- Has a strong community of users who share templates, which has helped drive adoption.
- Operates on a freemium model with Personal, Team, Business, and Enterprise tiers.
- Launched "Notion AI" features (integrating AI writing and assistance) in 2023.
- Has been valued highly as a venture-backed company;

brief.target_question: How do you choose the right headless CMS for your project?
brief.answer_first_paragraph: Choosing a headless CMS comes down to four variables: API style, hosting model, editor experience, and total cost of ownership, which typically runs from $0 for self-hosted open-source projects to over $50,000 per year for enterprise cloud plans with high traffic and editor seats. Match the CMS's content modeling depth and integration surface to the channels you actually serve today, not to the channels a vendor's sales deck claims you'll serve tomorrow.

sections.heading: What a headless CMS actually is (and is not)
sections.covers: Defines headless vs traditional coupled CMS vs hybrid/DXM, distinguishes content repository from presentation layer, and explains why the 'seamlessness' of an all-in-one platform carries hidden switching costs that only surface after launch.

sections.heading: The seven criteria that decide the shortlist
sections.covers: Walks through API style (REST vs GraphQL vs hybrid), content modeling flexibility, self-hosted vs managed hosting, editor UX, SDK and language coverage, ecosystem of plugins/integrations, and pricing model. Each criterion is given a one-line test the buyer can apply to any vendor.

sections.heading: Self-hosted vs cloud-hosted: the real trade-offs
sections.covers: Compares Strapi, Payload, Directus, and KeystoneJS (self-hosted, free license, you pay for infrastructure and DevOps) against Contentful, Sanity, Storyblok, and Hygraph (managed, you pay per seat, API call, and asset). Includes the operational overhead of self-hosting in hours per month.

sections.heading: Content modeling and schema flexibility
sections.covers: Why component-based modeling (Sanity, Storyblok, Payload) beats fixed page models for marketing teams, how blocks and references enable reuse across locales, and the cost of retrofitting a model after 200+ content items exist.

sections.heading: Developer experience and ecosystem
sections.covers: TypeScript support, local-first workflows, CLI tooling, preview environments, and webhook/plugin markets. References Payload's developer-first positioning from its YC launch and how that contrasts with marketer-first tools like Storyblok.

sections.heading: Total cost of ownership and the cost of seamlessness
sections.covers: Breaks down annual cost into seats ($0–$1000 per editor), API calls ($0.50–$5 per 1,000 above free tiers), assets/bandwidth, build minutes, and developer maintenance. Argues the 'cost of seamlessness' is vendor lock-in plus egress fees plus migration cost, which a 2023 vendor survey pegged at 3–9 months of engineering time for mid-size sites.

sections.heading: Migration, lock-in, and exit strategy
sections.covers: How to evaluate portability: open content format, export APIs, schema-as-code vs GUI-only, and whether the vendor has raised shutdown risk (analogous to Google's free service discontinuations). Includes a 10-point vendor due-diligence checklist.

content.brief.note: This is a specification, not copy. Doxa does not write the page — it states what the page has to contain to be citable.

content.charts.note: The page states 18 numeric values (18 years) and none is a measurement. Dates and version strings are temporal signals, not figures a model can cite you for — a Dataset of them would be valid and useless. Publishing percentages, amounts or magnitudes is the prerequisite.

phases.problem: Pages compete with each other for the same terms, splitting the signals between them.
AI crawlers are being refused, or robots.txt does not explicitly welcome the ones that produce citations. Nothing else in the programme can pay off until this is changed.
There is no reliable machine-readable statement of what these pages are about, so every fact has to be inferred from prose.
The basic metadata that decides how each page is titled, described and consolidated is incomplete.
The writing is not shaped for a model to answer from: the conclusion is buried, there is little concrete evidence, and the page does not chunk cleanly.
Nothing ties this site to a recognised entity — no consistent brand name across its own markup, and no links to the knowledge sources a model resolves entities against.
The site publishes none of the machine-facing files that state what it is and which pages matter.

proof_pass.purpose: Re-measure after the changes ship and diff the two signed audits, so the improvement is evidence rather than a claim.

estimate.basis: Doxa's own published per-call prices, summed over the services each phase needs for a single pass. It excludes the human work of making the changes, which is not ours to quote.

seo.engagement.note: This is a quote, not a commitment. The work spans your release cycle, so the figures are an estimate built from real prices and a real assessment — and every service named here is a public endpoint you can call yourself.

a2a.lede: OKX's second review gate is a live probe: a user registers, says "I would like to use the services of agent ID 9626", and the agent must answer. This is that exact flow, run against the live listing — task published, ASP connected, x402 agreed, payment settled, deliverable returned, job closed on-chain.
steps: User agent #8515 publishes a task to ASP #9626
Job 0xf9de475e…b8d6 — "Run the robots policy check for https://www.python.org/", budget 0.005 USDT, payment mode x402.
The ASP connects and the two agree terms
x402 agreement reached at the listed fee of 0.005 USDT — no renegotiation, the price the marketplace shows is the price charged.
Payment settles on X Layer before the work runs
HTTP 200, validation L3_REPRODUCED, 2/2 checks passed, Ed25519 signed. Ten AI crawlers evaluated against python.org's robots.txt, each with the rule that decided it.
The job closes on-chain and funds are released
tx 0x0bf430556041f128936f216b41d320a4a69d985cbf2596a77f915b9bfc9e49ed — "[x402 Job Completed] all steps complete."
a2a.note: The first attempt at this exposed a real defect and is worth stating: the buying agent's pre-check found no declared inputs, so it paid and sent an empty body, and 0.005 USDT bought an INVALID_INPUT. Two things changed as a result — every 402 challenge now declares its required inputs and a worked example, and a paid call that arrives empty returns that contract at HTTP 200 rather than an error, because the payment has already settled and charging for an error is indefensible.

examples: A 21-character title is correctly NOT flagged as short — the ported threshold is under 20, and an audit that cries wolf on a fine title is worse than one that says nothing.
A 52-character meta description IS flagged as short, against the same ported threshold of 80.
python.org's five H1 tags are reported as multiple; its 215 links are reported as too many against the threshold of 100.
Every image on the page has alt text, so no missing-alt fault is raised — the absence of a false alarm is checked as strictly as the presence of a true one.
python.org's robots.txt genuinely names no AI crawler, so all ten are correctly reported allowed rather than assumed blocked.
/llms.txt returns 404, so it is correctly reported missing.
geo.score equals the sum of its own signals, and the rubric weights total exactly 100.
Every figure published by content.charts was found verbatim in the source page; anything the model produced that the page does not state was discarded.

The thin-content word count is measured the way SEONaut's 200-word threshold was calibrated — skipping link text and stripping punctuation. python.org has 526 words of prose and 1,131 counted naively; applying a borrowed number to the wrong quantity is how a check stops firing.

Every measurable value found on the page was actually shown to the figure extractor. This is the invariant that broke when the extraction window was the first 4,000 characters and python.org's figures all began at character 4,006.
Numbers are classified before anything is asked of a model, and only measurements are charted. A page whose only numbers are dates gets a sentence explaining that, not an empty result.
